rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Employers must control health risks from welding fume even when welding is infrequent or limited in amount.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: All welding fume can cause lung cancer and can also cause asthma and other health conditions.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: A welding-fume risk assessment should consider the process, work volume, fume level, component size, metal and consumable.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Control should prioritise avoiding or reducing welding, then source-capture local exhaust ventilation, then suitable respiratory protection for residual exposure.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Local exhaust ventilation should capture fume at source and protect the welder and other people nearby.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Outdoor welding cannot normally rely on local exhaust ventilation and requires suitable respiratory protection.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Welding local-exhaust systems must be thoroughly examined and tested at least every 14 months, with examination records retained.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Respiratory health surveillance is required where assessment identifies a reasonable likelihood of occupational asthma, including relevant stainless-steel work.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Welding-fume risk depends on process, metal, coating, consumable, duration, ventilation, control performance, respiratory protection and worker susceptibility.

rows.source: HSE welding-fume control
rows.verified: Welding-fume evidence is process-, task-, workplace-, control-, worker- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level disease probability.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: An enclosed space is not designed for continuous worker occupancy and has limited entry or exit, inadequate ventilation, or both.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Ship operators should identify enclosed spaces, control access and avoid entry where reasonably possible.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: A competent person should complete a risk assessment before entry.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Entry requires preparation of the space, suitable controls and a permit-to-work system.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: The atmosphere must be tested before entry and monitored where conditions may change.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Rescue equipment, including suitable breathing apparatus, must be immediately available.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Emergency escape breathing devices are not suitable for enclosed-space entry or rescue.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Current MCA guidance requires drills and rescue procedures capable of addressing ship staff, shoreside staff and third parties.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Enclosed-space risk depends on space geometry, cargo or residues, atmosphere, isolation, ventilation, adjacent work, entry controls and rescue readiness.

rows.source: MCA enclosed-space safety on ships and fishing vessels
rows.verified: Enclosed-space evidence is vessel-, space-, atmosphere-, task-, crew- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fatality probability.
